blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Quote briefly and aptly, join evidence to comment with precise language, and build analytical paragraphs into one cohesive argument.

blocks.heading: Embedded quotation
blocks.text: An embedded quotation is a short quotation worked into the grammar of your own sentence, so the analysis and its evidence arrive together: "The verb ‘shrugged’ gives the river a body." The quotation is not dropped in as a standalone line; it is part of the sentence’s grammar, which is why the reader never has to leave your argument to find the evidence.

blocks.heading: Embedding a quotation
blocks.text: To embed a quotation: first choose a short phrase, the two or three words that carry the feature. Then fit it into your sentence’s grammar so it reads as part of your sentence — "The noun ‘rumour’ makes the rain sound half-believed" rather than "The rain is described in an interesting way. ‘Rain here is a rumour.’" Then comment on the words inside it, because the embedding exists so the comment can begin immediately.

blocks.heading: Why short works
blocks.text: Short quotations work because every word quoted can then be analysed: a two-word quotation leaves nowhere to hide, and the analysis either engages with those words or visibly fails to. A quoted sentence is mostly padding, and only two or three of its words were ever doing the work. A line reference is a location, not evidence: it tells a reader where to look but does not show the choice, and a range of lines ("lines 12–18") makes the reader do the finding that the analysis was supposed to do.

blocks.heading: The analytical paragraph
blocks.text: An analytical paragraph has four parts: a claim about the text, the evidence that shows it, the analysis of what the evidence does, and the link to the text’s purpose. In four moves: state the claim, quote the few words that show it, analyse what those words do to this reader, then say how that effect serves what the text is for. The four parts are a unit — a claim without evidence is assertion, evidence without analysis is quotation, and analysis without the link to purpose stops one sentence short of the mark.

blocks.heading: Verbs that join evidence to effect
blocks.text: Analytical verbs join evidence to effect precisely: suggests, conveys, evokes, positions, undercuts each say something different about how the choice works on the reader. "Suggests" leaves room and suits an implication; "positions" names what the writer does to the reader’s stance; "undercuts" says a later choice undoes an earlier one. The verb is where imprecision first creeps in, and where precision first shows.

blocks.heading: Precise effects and stock phrases
blocks.text: A stock phrase is one that could follow any quotation anywhere — "this engages the reader", "this creates a picture" — and it analyses nothing, because it was written for every text and so for none. A precise statement of effect could have been written for these words only: "the noun ‘rumour’ makes the rain sound half-believed, so the reader measures the dryness by the town’s scepticism." The reader it names is the text’s own audience — the worried resident, the browsing shopper — not a generic "reader" who exists nowhere.

blocks.heading: Worked example: a paragraph built properly
blocks.text: From a feature on a night market, four sentences: "The writer opens with the market’s noise rather than its name. ‘Frying onions, arguing, a baby somewhere’ places the reader inside the crowd before knowing where they stand. The list of three is all sense-impressions, so the reader is made to hear the market before being told about it. That sensory opening serves the piece’s purpose: it sells the market as an experience, which is what a reader deciding whether to visit is being asked to buy." Claim, evidence, analysis, link: the paragraph’s four parts in their order.

blocks.heading: From paragraphs to an argument
blocks.text: A coherent line of argument across a whole analysis is a single view of the text that each paragraph advances from a different side, joined by links that carry the reader from one to the next. An argument about a text organises its observations as evidence for a view; a list of observations sets them side by side and lets them add up, or not, by accident. The opening of the analysis states the view — the text’s purpose and its overall manner — and each paragraph after it is a witness for that view, so the reader leaves convinced of something rather than informed of many things.

blocks.heading: In the exam
blocks.text: The three analysis questions — Paper 1 Question 1(b), Paper 1 Question 2 and Paper 2’s reflective commentary — all reward the same habits taught here: short embedded quotations, precise effect statements named for the text’s own audience, and paragraphs that build one view of the text. The commentary on your own writing asks you to be your own analyst: quote your piece to yourself, and say what the words do. Practise the paragraph shape until it is the shape reached for under time pressure, because it is the unit every level table rewards.

blocks.heading: The observation string
blocks.text: The error is a string of separate observations with nothing joining them into a view of the text: "The writer uses a metaphor. The writer uses short sentences. The writer uses direct address." Each sentence may be true; together they say nothing, and they read as though the writer stopped at the collecting stage. The fix is the argument: decide what the text is doing to its reader, state it, and make each observation evidence for it — the metaphor, the short sentences and the direct address may all be witnesses to the same urgent purpose, and the analysis is what shows it.
